newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian shares edge up, seen firmer.[CORRECTED 11:05 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Russian shares edge up, seen firmer.[CORRECTED 11:05 GMT]

text.p: Leading Russian shares firmed in early trade on Wednesday after a weak start to the day, and traders saw the market closing firmer on sustained local and foreign demand.
The Russian Trading System 22-share index opened slightly off at 338.93 after closing on Tuesday at 339.04.
But traders saw the market picking up towards the end of the day although a correction was possible.
"I think a lot of people would like to see the market drift a bit lower as there are quite a few unsatisfied orders in blue chip stocks," said Martin Diggle, director at Brunswick.
"But I don't think it will move very much lower because there's quite a lot of demand, especially for blue chips. I would expect to see the index close slightly higher."
National power company UES rose to $0.2773 at GMT 0830 from $0.2750 on Tuesday and regional power utility Mosenergo edged up to $1.354 from $1.351. Automotive producer Kamaz rose to $1.50 from $1.46.

"It's a bull market (Corrects description of market). There was a little correction in the morning, but the market is growing," said Alexander Fonarkov, a trader at Regent European Securities, adding that second tier stocks were also doing well.
Traders said the Russian market would continue to benefit from the optimism fueling recent gains on Western markets.
The Dow Jones closed at an all-time high 7225.32 on Tuesday despite signs of slowing in the short term.

"There is a new flow of funds into Russia from Western investors, positive global equity and bond markets, which is supportive, and a perception that the fundamental situation in Russia is improving politically and economically," said Diggle.

But some traders said major investors would hold back until the results of a U.S. Federal Reserve meeting on May 20 are announced. Investors are worried the Fed may decide to raise interest rates, which would make investment in equities less attractive.
"We'll definitely see some money from the West as well as from locals," Fonarkov said. "But big money will not flow in until the situation in the U.S. with interest rates becomes clear."
